dx: Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella henselae) in advanced HIV infection
case: A 41-year-old man with HIV infection who stopped antiretroviral therapy 2 years ago comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of enlarging red-purple skin nodules on his trunk and arms. He also has night sweats and a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss. He recently adopted a kitten. Temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows 12 dome-shaped, friable, vascular nodules from 3 to 15 mm across that bleed with minor trauma. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 38/mm3 (normal 500 to 1500). Biopsy of a nodule and blood PCR confirm bacillary angiomatosis caused by Bartonella henselae.

questions.stem: Kaposi sarcoma was the leading alternative diagnosis before the biopsy. Which of the following microscopic findings in his biopsy specimen best distinguishes his lesion from Kaposi sarcoma?
options: Spindle cells lining slit-like vascular spaces
Lymphocytes and plasma cells around vessels
Neutrophils with silver-staining bacilli
Extravasated red cells and hemosiderin
approach: Both lesions are red-purple vascular nodules in a patient with very low CD4 counts, so the gross appearance cannot separate them.
Bacillary angiomatosis is an infection-driven capillary proliferation, so look for acute inflammation and organisms.
Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8 driven spindle cell tumor with lymphocytes and plasma cells and no neutrophils.
questions.why: Bacillary angiomatosis shows lobules of small capillaries lined by plump endothelial cells, with neutrophils, nuclear debris, and purple clumps of bacteria. The bacilli stain black with a Warthin-Starry silver stain. Neutrophils plus organisms point to an infection, which is why the lesions resolve with antibiotics such as a macrolide or doxycycline. Kaposi sarcoma lacks both neutrophils and bacteria.
whyNot: Spindle cells forming slit-like spaces are the hallmark of Kaposi sarcoma, the lesion this finding would favor.
A lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltrate is typical of Kaposi sarcoma, not of bacillary angiomatosis.
Correct.
Leaked red cells and hemosiderin are classic in Kaposi sarcoma and can appear in any bleeding vascular lesion, so they do not favor infection.

questions.stem: He restarts antiretroviral therapy. Twelve months later, his CD4+ count is 410/mm3. A cousin with AIDS and HHV-8 associated Kaposi sarcoma also restarted therapy, and her skin lesions have shrunk without chemotherapy. Which of the following best explains the regression of her Kaposi sarcoma lesions?
options: Restored T-cell control of HHV-8 infected cells
Direct inhibition of HHV-8 DNA polymerase by the drugs
Rising IL-6 levels that induce endothelial apoptosis
Neutrophil clearance of Bartonella in the lesions
approach: Kaposi sarcoma is driven by HHV-8, a herpesvirus that persists in latently infected cells.
Cytotoxic T cells normally keep HHV-8 infected cells in check, and AIDS removes that surveillance.
When therapy restores CD4+ T cells, cell-mediated control returns and the virus-driven lesions shrink.
questions.why: HHV-8 infected spindle cells express viral proteins that promote growth and angiogenesis. In healthy people, CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, helped by CD4+ T cells, kill these cells and keep the infection latent. Profound CD4+ depletion in AIDS or in transplant immunosuppression removes this control, so Kaposi sarcoma grows. When antiretroviral therapy rebuilds the CD4+ pool, T-cell surveillance recovers and many lesions regress, the same reason lowering immunosuppression helps transplant recipients.
whyNot: Correct.
Antiretroviral drugs target HIV enzymes. They have no meaningful activity against HHV-8 replication.
IL-6 is a growth signal in HHV-8 disease (the virus even encodes its own IL-6 homolog), and IL-6 from atrial myxoma causes fever and weight loss. It does not kill tumor cells.
Bartonella causes bacillary angiomatosis, not Kaposi sarcoma, and neutrophils play no role in controlling HHV-8.

questions.stem: Echocardiography shows a small aortic valve vegetation. Three sets of routine blood cultures are negative after 5 days of incubation. Which of the following properties of his organism best explains the negative cultures?
options: Absence of a cell wall, so it cannot be Gram stained
Obligate intracellular growth that rules out agar culture
Spirochete form too thin to see by light microscopy
Slow fastidious growth that needs special media and time
approach: Recognize Bartonella as a classic cause of culture-negative endocarditis, with HACEK organisms and Coxiella burnetii.
Ask why each group escapes routine culture: fastidious growth, or obligate intracellular life.
Bartonella is a fastidious, facultative intracellular gram-negative rod that grows on enriched agar only after weeks.
questions.why: Bartonella henselae and Bartonella quintana are small gram-negative bacilli that grow very slowly and need enriched media and prolonged incubation, so standard blood cultures read at 5 days are negative. Diagnosis rests on serology, PCR, or Warthin-Starry staining of valve tissue. HACEK organisms are also fastidious. Coxiella burnetii is classically described as obligate intracellular and is diagnosed by serology.
whyNot: A missing cell wall describes Mycoplasma. Bartonella has a gram-negative cell wall, and Gram staining is unrelated to whether a culture grows.
Obligate intracellular growth describes Coxiella burnetii, rickettsiae, and chlamydiae. Bartonella is facultative and does grow on enriched agar, slowly.
Thin spirochetes such as Treponema are hard to see, but Bartonella is a small rod, and visibility on a stain does not explain negative cultures.
Correct.

questions.stem: An inguinal lymph node is biopsied to exclude lymphoma. Given his CD4+ count, which of the following regions of the node is most likely to show the greatest loss of lymphocytes?
options: Germinal centers of the cortical follicles
Paracortex between follicles and medulla
Medullary cords near the hilum
Subcapsular sinus beneath the capsule
approach: Identify the cells that are depleted: CD4+ T lymphocytes.
Recall where T cells live in a lymph node: the paracortex, which contains high endothelial venules.
B cells sit in cortical follicles and plasma cells in medullary cords, so those areas are less affected.
questions.why: A lymph node has an outer cortex with B-cell follicles, a deeper paracortex where T cells meet dendritic cells, and a medulla with cords of plasma cells and macrophages. Lymphocytes enter the paracortex from blood through high endothelial venules. Loss of CD4+ T cells in late HIV infection empties the paracortex. The thymus is where T cells mature and are selected, while B cells mature in the bone marrow.
whyNot: Germinal centers are B-cell zones. They are often hyperplastic early in HIV and later involute, but they are not the T-cell area.
Correct.
Medullary cords hold plasma cells and macrophages, not the main T-cell population.
The subcapsular sinus is a lymph channel lined by macrophages where afferent lymph enters. It is not a lymphocyte zone.

dx: Stress (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy after sudden bereavement in a postmenopausal woman
case: A 66-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the onset of crushing substernal chest pain and shortness of breath. The pain began shortly after she learned that her husband had died suddenly. She has no history of heart disease. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg. An ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads V2 to V5. Serum troponin I is 2.4 ng/mL (normal less than 0.04). Emergency coronary angiography shows no obstructive coronary disease. Left ventriculography shows akinetic, ballooned apical segments with vigorously contracting basal segments and an ejection fraction of 35% (normal 55 to 70). Diagnosis: stress (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: Her family asks what will happen to her heart muscle. Which of the following is the most likely course of her left ventricular wall motion?
options: Return to normal wall motion within weeks
Fibrous apical scar with a lasting aneurysm
Progressive dilation of all four chambers
Progressive concentric thickening of the septum
approach: Note the clues: sudden emotional stress, ST elevation and troponin rise, but no blocked coronary artery.
Recognize stress cardiomyopathy as catecholamine-related stunning of apical myocytes, not infarction.
Stunned myocardium recovers, so wall motion usually returns to normal within days to weeks.
questions.why: In stress (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy, a surge of catecholamines causes transient dysfunction of the apical segments, which recover once the surge passes. Little myocyte death occurs, so there is no large scar. Ejection fraction typically normalizes within about 1 to 4 weeks. Acute risks still include heart failure, shock, arrhythmia, and apical thrombus, so patients are watched closely early on.
whyNot: Correct.
A fibrous scar with aneurysm follows a transmural infarction from coronary occlusion, which angiography ruled out.
Four-chamber dilation describes dilated cardiomyopathy, as seen after viral myocarditis or with alcohol, not a stress-induced stunning.
Concentric septal thickening describes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or pressure overload, not this transient apical dysfunction.

questions.stem: Catecholamines acting on beta-1 adrenergic receptors make her basal segments contract and relax vigorously. Protein kinase A phosphorylates troponin I in these myocytes. Which of the following is the direct effect of this phosphorylation?
options: Stronger tropomyosin binding to actin, blocking cross-bridges
Higher troponin C affinity for Ca2+, prolonging binding
Inhibition of myosin ATPase, slowing cross-bridge cycling
Lower troponin C affinity for Ca2+, speeding relaxation
approach: Trace the pathway: beta-1 receptor, Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, protein kinase A.
List the PKA targets: L-type Ca2+ channels, phospholamban, and troponin I.
Phosphorylated troponin I makes troponin C let go of Ca2+ sooner, so relaxation is faster.
questions.why: Beta-1 stimulation raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A. PKA phosphorylates L-type Ca2+ channels (more Ca2+ entry and stronger contraction), phospholamban (releasing its brake on SERCA2a so the sarcoplasmic reticulum takes up Ca2+ faster), and troponin I. Phosphorylated troponin I lowers the Ca2+ affinity of troponin C, so Ca2+ comes off the myofilaments faster. Together these speed relaxation, which matters at high heart rates when diastole is short.
whyNot: Tropomyosin position is controlled by Ca2+ binding to troponin C, and PKA does not make tropomyosin block actin.
Higher affinity would slow relaxation. This is the opposite of what phosphorylated troponin I does.
PKA does not inhibit myosin ATPase. Sympathetic stimulation speeds cross-bridge cycling.
Correct.

questions.stem: Three days later, her blood pressure is 92/60 mm Hg, and an intravenous fluid bolus is given. Her stroke volume rises as left ventricular end-diastolic volume increases. Which of the following best explains how her cardiac muscle grades its force in this response?
options: More motor units are recruited within the ventricular wall
Stretch improves filament overlap and troponin C Ca2+ sensitivity
Higher stimulation frequency causes tetanic summation of twitches
Stretch opens more gap junctions between ventricular myocytes
approach: More filling stretches the sarcomeres, which is the Frank-Starling mechanism.
At the sarcomere, stretch moves cardiac muscle toward optimal overlap and increases troponin C sensitivity to Ca2+.
Cardiac muscle cannot recruit motor units or tetanize, because every myocyte contracts with each beat and the long refractory period prevents summation.
questions.why: Resting cardiac sarcomeres sit below their optimal length, so added preload brings actin and myosin closer to ideal overlap. Stretch also increases the Ca2+ sensitivity of troponin C. Both raise the force of the next beat. Skeletal muscle grades force differently, by recruiting motor units and by summing twitches up to tetanus.
whyNot: Motor unit recruitment grades force in skeletal muscle. The heart is a functional syncytium, and all myocytes contract every beat.
Correct.
Tetanic summation happens in skeletal muscle. The long cardiac refractory period prevents it in the heart.
Gap junctions couple myocytes electrically at all times. Stretch does not grade force by opening more of them.

questions.stem: Her heart function returns to normal. Two years later, she has chest pressure when climbing stairs. Coronary angiography again shows no stenosis. Echocardiography shows a calcified aortic valve with an area of 0.7 cm2 (normal 3 to 4) and left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following best explains her new exertional chest pain?
options: Repeated catecholamine stunning of the apex
Spasm of the epicardial coronary arteries
Myocardial oxygen demand exceeding supply
Emboli from the valve to the coronary arteries
approach: Coronary atherosclerosis causes most angina, but her arteries are clear, so look for another cause of ischemia.
Severe aortic stenosis forces the ventricle to generate high pressure, and the thick wall needs more oxygen.
High wall stress and end-diastolic pressure squeeze subendocardial vessels, so supply falls as demand rises.
questions.why: Most ischemic heart disease comes from coronary atherosclerosis, but ischemia also occurs when demand outstrips supply in open arteries. In severe aortic stenosis, the hypertrophied ventricle has more muscle to feed and works against a high pressure. Raised diastolic wall pressure compresses subendocardial vessels, and exertion shortens diastole when the coronaries fill. The result is classic exertional angina with normal angiograms.
whyNot: Stress cardiomyopathy follows an acute emotional or physical stressor and causes rest symptoms with wall motion changes, not predictable exertional pain.
Vasospasm causes angina at rest, often at night, and would not explain pain tied to exertion in a patient with a tight aortic valve.
Correct.
Calcific emboli to the coronaries are rare and would cause sudden infarction, not repeated exertional pain.

topics: Causes of ischemia with normal coronaries

dx: Acute mitral regurgitation from posteromedial papillary muscle rupture after an inferior myocardial infarction
case: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of sudden severe shortness of breath. Four days ago, he had 2 days of chest pain that he did not report. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 122/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 84/52 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. Crackles are heard over both lung fields, and a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex. An ECG shows Q waves in leads II, III, and aVF. Echocardiography shows a flail posterior mitral leaflet attached to a ruptured posteromedial papillary muscle, severe mitral regurgitation, a normal-sized left atrium, and an ejection fraction of 60%. Diagnosis: acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture after an inferior myocardial infarction.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his sudden pulmonary edema despite a normal ejection fraction?
options: Loss of left ventricular contractility from the infarct
Increased pulmonary capillary permeability from sepsis
Right ventricular failure from the inferior infarction
Sudden backflow into a small, stiff left atrium
approach: Notice the normal ejection fraction and normal-sized left atrium with severe regurgitation.
A left atrium that has not had time to dilate cannot absorb a large regurgitant volume, so its pressure soars.
High left atrial pressure passes back to the pulmonary capillaries and floods the alveoli, while forward stroke volume falls and pressure drops.
questions.why: In acute mitral regurgitation, part of each stroke volume goes backward into a small, stiff left atrium. Left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rise abruptly, producing cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Forward output falls, causing hypotension and shock. The ejection fraction looks normal or high because the ventricle empties into two low-resistance outlets. Chronic regurgitation is better tolerated because the atrium dilates and becomes more compliant over time.
whyNot: His ejection fraction is 60%, so pump failure from a large infarct does not explain the edema.
Increased permeability describes noncardiogenic edema such as ARDS. Nothing suggests sepsis, and the new murmur points to a mechanical cause.
Right ventricular infarction causes hypotension with clear lungs and raised jugular pressure, not pulmonary edema.
Correct.

questions.stem: Coronary angiography shows occlusion of the right coronary artery proximal to the origin of the posterior descending artery. Which of the following best explains why the posteromedial papillary muscle, rather than the anterolateral one, ruptured?
options: It is thinner and anchors fewer chordae tendineae
It depends on a single artery, the posterior descending
It is supplied by end branches of the anterior descending
It lies over the septum and is stressed by septal motion
approach: Determine dominance: the posterior descending artery comes from the right coronary artery, so he is right dominant.
Recall the papillary muscle supply: anterolateral from both the LAD and circumflex, posteromedial from the posterior descending artery alone.
A muscle with one source of blood infarcts completely when that source is blocked.
questions.why: Coronary dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the posterior descending artery, the right coronary artery in most people. The anterolateral papillary muscle receives a dual supply from the left anterior descending and left circumflex arteries, so it rarely infarcts completely. The posteromedial papillary muscle usually depends only on the posterior descending artery. An inferior infarction from right coronary occlusion can therefore kill it, and rupture follows several days later as the necrotic muscle softens.
whyNot: Muscle size and chordal count do not explain the pattern. The key difference is blood supply.
Correct.
The left anterior descending artery helps supply the anterolateral muscle, and that muscle's dual supply is what protects it.
Both papillary muscles arise from the ventricular free wall region. Rupture follows ischemic necrosis, not septal motion.

questions.stem: Papillary muscle rupture occurred at the stage of healing when macrophages are removing necrotic myocardium. Which of the following complications of infarction most typically occurs in this same time window?
options: Ventricular free wall rupture with cardiac tamponade
Ventricular fibrillation in the first hour after occlusion
Dressler syndrome with fever and pericardial effusion
True ventricular aneurysm containing mural thrombus
approach: Place the macrophage phase on the timeline: about 3 to 7 days after infarction.
At this point the necrotic wall is softest, before collagen is laid down.
Complications that tear tissue (papillary muscle, septal, and free wall rupture) cluster here.
questions.why: From about day 3 to day 7, macrophages clear dead myocytes and granulation tissue has only begun to form, so the infarcted wall is at its weakest. Papillary muscle rupture, interventricular septal rupture, and free wall rupture all peak in this window. Free wall rupture fills the pericardial sac with blood and causes tamponade. Early arrhythmias peak in the first hours, and aneurysm and Dressler syndrome come weeks later.
whyNot: Correct.
Ventricular fibrillation is most common in the first hours of ischemia, before the macrophage phase.
Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis that appears weeks after the infarct.
A true aneurysm forms from a thin fibrous scar, weeks to months after a transmural infarct.

questions.stem: His infarct began when the right coronary artery was suddenly occluded by thrombus. Which of the following events in the ischemic myocytes marks the change from reversible to irreversible injury after about 20 to 40 minutes?
options: Glycogen depletion from anaerobic glycolysis
Loss of contractility as ATP levels fall
Membrane rupture with Ca2+ influx
Cell swelling from Na+/K+-ATPase failure
approach: Recall the early sequence: ATP falls, glycolysis takes over, lactate builds, and contraction stops within about a minute.
These early changes reverse if flow returns quickly.
Irreversible injury is marked by severe membrane damage, Ca2+ influx, and mitochondrial amorphous densities.
questions.why: Within a minute of occlusion, myocytes lose contractility as aerobic ATP production fails. They switch to anaerobic glycolysis, deplete glycogen, accumulate lactate, and swell as the Na+/K+-ATPase falters. All of this can reverse if blood flow returns. After about 20 to 40 minutes, plasma and mitochondrial membranes are badly damaged, Ca2+ floods the cell and its mitochondria, and the cell dies. Necrosis then spreads as a wavefront from subendocardium to epicardium over several hours.
whyNot: Glycogen depletion begins within minutes and is reversible if flow is restored.
Contractility is lost within about 60 seconds, long before injury is irreversible.
Correct.
Swelling from pump failure is a reversible change.

dx: Constrictive pericarditis after mediastinal radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma
case: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of increasing abdominal girth, leg swelling, and fatigue. At age 24, she received mediastinal radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 106/72 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is 15 cm H2O (normal less than 8) and rises further with inspiration. An early diastolic sound is heard at the left sternal border. The liver is enlarged, and ascites and pitting edema of both legs are present. CT shows a pericardium thickened to 7 mm (normal about 2 or less) with patchy calcification. Diagnosis: constrictive pericarditis due to prior radiation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the rise in her jugular venous pressure during inspiration?
options: Inspiration compresses the heart through a stiff pericardial sac
A rigid pericardium keeps the right heart from accepting more return
Fluid in the pericardial sac shifts to the right heart on inspiration
Inspiration raises pulmonary resistance and right ventricular afterload
approach: Normally, inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, pulls blood into the right heart, and the jugular pressure falls.
A thick, calcified pericardium fixes the volume of the heart and does not transmit the falling intrathoracic pressure.
The extra venous return cannot enter, so it backs up and jugular pressure rises (Kussmaul sign).
questions.why: Constrictive pericarditis encases the heart in a rigid shell, so diastolic filling stops abruptly once the chambers reach the shell's volume. On inspiration, venous return to the thorax increases, but the right heart cannot expand to take it, and the fall in intrathoracic pressure is not passed to the chambers. Jugular pressure therefore rises instead of falling. This Kussmaul sign, a pericardial knock, and calcification after radiation, tuberculosis, or surgery are the classic findings.
whyNot: The rigid sac fixes heart volume. It does not actively compress the heart more during inspiration.
Correct.
Constriction involves a thick, scarred pericardium with little or no fluid. Effusion with tamponade usually causes pulsus paradoxus without a Kussmaul sign.
Pulmonary resistance changes little during quiet inspiration and would not raise jugular pressure in this way.

questions.stem: Her jugular venous pulse is examined closely. Which of the following waveform features is most likely to be present?
options: Large, broad v waves
Cannon a waves
Steep y descent
Absent y descent
approach: The y descent reflects rapid filling of the right ventricle after the tricuspid valve opens.
In constriction, early diastolic filling is fast because atrial pressure is high and the ventricle is not yet stiff-limited.
Filling then stops abruptly at the pericardial limit, so the y descent is steep and deep.
questions.why: The jugular a wave comes from atrial contraction, the c wave from tricuspid bulging at the start of systole, and the v wave from atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve. The x descent follows atrial relaxation, and the y descent follows tricuspid opening. In constrictive pericarditis, high atrial pressure drives very rapid early filling, so the y descent is prominent, then filling halts when the pericardium stops further expansion. In tamponade, fluid compresses the heart throughout diastole, so the y descent is blunted.
whyNot: Large v waves suggest tricuspid regurgitation, where ventricular blood fills the atrium during systole.
Cannon a waves occur when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, as in complete heart block or other AV dissociation.
Correct.
A blunted or absent y descent is typical of cardiac tamponade, where fluid limits filling throughout diastole.

questions.stem: She undergoes pericardiectomy. To free the great arteries from the thickened pericardium, the surgeon passes a finger directly behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk and in front of the superior vena cava. Which of the following spaces does the finger enter?
options: Transverse pericardial sinus
Oblique pericardial sinus
Costomediastinal pleural recess
Anterior mediastinal space
approach: Use the landmarks: behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the superior vena cava.
Recall the two pericardial sinuses formed by reflections of serous pericardium.
The transverse sinus separates the arterial outflow from the venous inflow at the top of the heart.
questions.why: The serous pericardium reflects around the great vessels in two sleeves, one around the aorta and pulmonary trunk and one around the veins. The gap between the arterial and venous sleeves is the transverse pericardial sinus, which lies behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk and in front of the superior vena cava. Surgeons pass a finger or clamp through it to isolate the great arteries. The oblique sinus is a blind pocket behind the left atrium, bounded by the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava.
whyNot: Correct.
The oblique sinus lies behind the left atrium between the pulmonary veins, not behind the great arteries.
The costomediastinal recess is part of the pleural cavity along the anterior lung margin, outside the pericardium.
The anterior mediastinum lies between the sternum and the pericardium, in front of the great vessels.

questions.stem: Before surgery, her physicians considered restrictive cardiomyopathy, since radiation can also cause that disorder. Which of the following findings would have favored restrictive cardiomyopathy over constrictive pericarditis?
options: Septal shift with respiration on echocardiography
Pericardial calcification on chest imaging
Early diastolic pericardial knock on auscultation
Low QRS voltage with thick ventricular walls
approach: Both conditions impair diastolic filling and cause right-sided congestion, so look for a finding that points to the myocardium.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy comes from a stiff, infiltrated, or fibrotic muscle; constriction comes from a stiff shell.
Low voltage despite thick walls means the wall is thickened by deposits, the classic sign of cardiac amyloidosis.
questions.why: Restrictive cardiomyopathy stiffens the myocardium itself, from amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, radiation fibrosis, endomyocardial fibrosis, or Loeffler endocarditis. In amyloidosis, the walls look thick but the ECG voltage is low, because the added mass is protein, not muscle. Constrictive pericarditis instead features a thick or calcified pericardium, a knock, and marked respiratory interdependence of the ventricles. Telling them apart matters because constriction is cured by pericardiectomy.
whyNot: Respiratory septal shift reflects ventricular interdependence inside a fixed shell, a feature of constriction.
Pericardial calcification indicates constrictive pericarditis, not a myocardial disease.
A pericardial knock comes from abrupt halt of filling by a rigid pericardium and favors constriction.
Correct.

dx: Libman-Sacks endocarditis and fibrinous pericarditis in systemic lupus erythematosus
case: A 29-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus comes to the physician because of 5 days of sharp chest pain that worsens when she lies down and eases when she sits forward. She also has joint pain and a facial rash. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg. A three-component friction rub is heard. Laboratory studies show high anti-double-stranded DNA antibody titers, a low serum C3 of 52 mg/dL (normal 90 to 180), and positive anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies. Three sets of blood cultures are negative. Echocardiography shows a small pericardial effusion and several small vegetations on the mitral leaflets. Diagnosis: Libman-Sacks endocarditis and pericarditis due to lupus.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the mitral valve lesions that would be seen on pathologic examination?
options: Small warty nodules along lines of closure only
Bulky friable vegetations full of bacterial colonies
Small sterile vegetations on both leaflet surfaces
Nodular calcification of the mitral annulus
approach: Blood cultures are negative and the vegetations are small, so this is a noninfective endocarditis.
Libman-Sacks lesions in lupus are small, sterile, and can sit on either or both surfaces of the leaflets.
Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis and rheumatic vegetations sit on the lines of closure.
questions.why: Libman-Sacks endocarditis produces small, sterile, flat or warty vegetations, most often on the mitral valve. Unlike most other vegetations, they can form on the undersurface of the leaflet and on the chordae as well as the atrial surface. The underlying valve shows inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis and may later scar and regurgitate. Infective vegetations are bulky, friable, and full of organisms, and nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis in cancer forms bland vegetations along the closure lines.
whyNot: Small vegetations restricted to the lines of closure describe acute rheumatic fever or nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis.
Bulky, friable, organism-filled vegetations define infective endocarditis, which the negative cultures argue against.
Correct.
Mitral annular calcification is a degenerative change of older adults and is unrelated to lupus or to vegetations.

questions.stem: If her pericardium were examined, which of the following types of exudate would most likely be found?
options: Purulent exudate rich in neutrophils
Caseous exudate with granulomas
Hemorrhagic exudate with tumor cells
Fibrinous or serofibrinous exudate
approach: Identify the cause: lupus, an immune complex disease.
Immune-mediated pericarditis leaks plasma proteins, so fibrin and some serous fluid collect on the surfaces.
Match other exudate types to their causes: bacteria for purulent, tuberculosis for caseous, cancer for hemorrhagic.
questions.why: Lupus pericarditis is driven by immune complex deposition and complement activation, which make pericardial vessels leaky. Fibrinogen escapes and forms a shaggy fibrin coat, often with a small serous effusion, and the rough surfaces cause the friction rub. The same fibrinous or serofibrinous pattern follows uremia, rheumatic fever, early infarction, Dressler syndrome, and radiation. Purulent, caseous, and hemorrhagic patterns point to bacteria, tuberculosis, and cancer.
whyNot: Purulent pericarditis follows bacterial infection, often by spread from pneumonia, and causes high fever and rigors.
Caseous pericarditis is typical of tuberculosis and can progress to constriction.
Hemorrhagic pericarditis is most often due to metastatic cancer or tuberculosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: One year later, she is pregnant. Her anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies remain positive. Which of the following fetal conditions is she at increased risk of having?
options: Transposition of the great arteries
Congenital complete heart block
Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
Patent ductus arteriosus
approach: Anti-Ro antibodies are IgG, which crosses the placenta in the second trimester.
These antibodies bind fetal cardiac tissue and inflame and scar the conduction system, especially the AV node.
The result is an immune-mediated, often permanent, heart block in a structurally normal heart.
questions.why: Maternal anti-Ro (SSA) and sometimes anti-La (SSB) IgG antibodies cross the placenta and target fetal cardiac cells, causing inflammation and fibrosis of the AV node. The fetus develops congenital complete heart block, usually detected as fetal bradycardia between about 18 and 24 weeks. The risk is about 1 to 2% in mothers with these antibodies. This is one of several immune-mediated heart diseases, along with Libman-Sacks endocarditis and Dressler syndrome.
whyNot: Transposition of the great arteries is linked to maternal diabetes, not to anti-Ro antibodies.
Correct.
Ebstein anomaly is linked to maternal lithium use.
Patent ductus arteriosus is linked to congenital rubella and prematurity.

questions.stem: Her vegetations are on the mitral leaflets, which open and close with each cardiac cycle. Which of the following events marks the moment her mitral valve opens?
options: LV pressure falls below atrial pressure in early diastole
LV pressure rises above atrial pressure in early systole
Atrial contraction raises atrial pressure late in diastole
LV pressure falls below aortic pressure, ending ejection
approach: Valves open and close only in response to pressure differences across them.
After the aortic valve closes, the ventricle relaxes with both valves shut (isovolumetric relaxation).
When left ventricular pressure drops below left atrial pressure, the mitral valve opens and rapid filling begins.
questions.why: Each valve opens when pressure upstream exceeds pressure downstream. The aortic valve closes when ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, producing S2 and starting isovolumetric relaxation. Ventricular pressure keeps falling with both valves closed until it drops below left atrial pressure, and then the mitral valve opens and rapid filling begins. The mitral valve closes again when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure at the start of systole, producing S1.
whyNot: Correct.
This event closes the mitral valve at the start of isovolumetric contraction and produces S1.
Atrial contraction happens late in diastole, when the mitral valve is already open.
This event closes the aortic valve and produces S2. The mitral valve is still shut.

dx: Adenovirus myocarditis with heart failure and ventricular arrhythmia in a college student
case: A 20-year-old man who is a college student is brought to the emergency department because of 4 days of shortness of breath, palpitations, and chest discomfort. Two weeks ago, he had fever, sore throat, and red, watery eyes that resolved without treatment. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 98/64 mm Hg. Crackles are heard at both lung bases, and an S3 is present. Serum troponin I is 4.8 ng/mL (normal less than 0.04). Telemetry shows runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia. Echocardiography shows global hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of 30% (normal 55 to 70). Coronary angiography is normal. Endomyocardial biopsy PCR detects adenovirus DNA. Diagnosis: adenovirus myocarditis.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is most likely on light microscopy of his endomyocardial biopsy specimen?
options: Lymphocytic infiltrate with nearby myocyte necrosis
Eosinophil-rich infiltrate around small vessels
Multinucleated giant cells with widespread necrosis
Noncaseating granulomas with patchy fibrosis
approach: Recognize the pattern: a young adult with heart failure and arrhythmia shortly after a viral illness.
Viral myocarditis causes injury by the virus and by the cell-mediated immune response to infected myocytes.
The Dallas criteria pattern is a lymphocytic infiltrate with damage to adjacent myocytes.
questions.why: Viral myocarditis shows patchy lymphocytes, mostly T cells, in the interstitium with necrosis of adjacent myocytes. Viruses such as coxsackie B and adenovirus infect myocytes directly, and the immune attack on infected cells adds to the damage. The injury raises troponin, weakens contraction, and creates foci for ventricular arrhythmias. Many patients recover, but some progress to dilated cardiomyopathy.
whyNot: Correct.
Eosinophils suggest hypersensitivity myocarditis from a drug, or a hypereosinophilic process.
Giant cells with extensive necrosis indicate giant cell myocarditis, a rare, rapidly fatal autoimmune form.
Noncaseating granulomas point to cardiac sarcoidosis, which classically causes heart block.

questions.stem: Adenovirus enters cardiomyocytes by binding a transmembrane protein at the intercalated discs. It shares this receptor with another classic viral cause of myocarditis. Which of the following viruses uses the same receptor?
options: Parvovirus B19
Influenza A virus
Coxsackievirus B
Human herpesvirus 6
approach: Recall the receptor named for its two viruses: the coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor (CAR).
CAR is a junctional adhesion protein concentrated at intercalated discs in heart muscle.
Each of the other viruses causes myocarditis but enters cells through a different receptor.
questions.why: The coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor (CAR) is a transmembrane protein in cell junctions and is abundant at cardiac intercalated discs. Coxsackie B virus, the classic cause of viral myocarditis, and several adenovirus types both use it to enter myocytes, which helps explain why both target the heart. Other causes of myocarditis include parvovirus B19, HHV-6, Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease), Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease), diphtheria toxin, drug hypersensitivity, and lupus.
whyNot: Parvovirus B19 causes myocarditis by infecting endothelial cells and binds globoside (P antigen), not CAR.
Influenza A binds sialic acid residues and only occasionally causes myocarditis.
Correct.
Human herpesvirus 6 can cause myocarditis but uses other receptors, such as CD46 for HHV-6A.

questions.stem: Three weeks later, his ejection fraction is still 25%, and the left ventricle is dilated. He suddenly develops weakness of the right arm and difficulty speaking. His heart rhythm is sinus. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his new symptoms?
options: Paradoxical embolus from a deep vein thrombus
Septic embolus from an infected heart valve
Lacunar infarct from small vessel hyalinosis
Embolus from a ventricular mural thrombus
approach: Sudden aphasia with right arm weakness means a left middle cerebral artery territory stroke, most often embolic.
A dilated, poorly contracting ventricle has slow, stagnant flow, one part of Virchow triad.
Thrombus forms on the akinetic wall and can embolize to the brain even in sinus rhythm.
questions.why: Heart failure with a low ejection fraction lets blood stagnate in a dilated left ventricle, especially near akinetic segments, and injured endocardium adds a thrombogenic surface. A mural thrombus can form and fragment, sending emboli to the brain, kidneys, spleen, or limbs. Other complications of heart failure include pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiorenal syndrome, and cardiac cachexia.
whyNot: A paradoxical embolus needs a venous thrombus and a right-to-left shunt such as a patent foramen ovale, and neither is described.
Septic emboli come from infective endocarditis, which is not present.
Lacunar infarcts come from long-standing hypertension or diabetes and classically cause pure motor or pure sensory deficits. They do not cause aphasia, which is a cortical sign.
Correct.

questions.stem: His weak contraction reflects loss and dysfunction of myocytes. In a healthy cardiomyocyte, Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum must act on the myofilaments before contraction can begin. Which of the following events directly allows myosin heads to bind actin?
options: Ca2+ binds calmodulin, activating myosin light chain kinase
Ca2+ binds troponin C, shifting tropomyosin off actin sites
Ca2+ binds troponin I, which then phosphorylates myosin
ATP binds the myosin head, cocking it toward actin
approach: Place this step in the sequence: L-type Ca2+ entry, Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release through RyR2, then Ca2+ binding to the myofilaments.
In striated muscle, tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin at rest.
Ca2+ binding to troponin C changes the troponin complex and rolls tropomyosin away, so cross-bridges can form.
questions.why: In cardiac and skeletal muscle, the thin filament carries tropomyosin and the troponin complex (troponin C, I, and T). At rest, tropomyosin blocks the myosin-binding sites on actin. When cytosolic Ca2+ rises, it binds troponin C, which pulls troponin I off actin and lets tropomyosin slide away. Myosin heads then bind actin and cycle as long as Ca2+ and ATP are available.
whyNot: Calmodulin activating myosin light chain kinase is how smooth muscle starts contraction, not cardiac muscle.
Correct.
Troponin I is an inhibitory subunit, not a kinase, and Ca2+ binds troponin C, not troponin I.
ATP binding detaches myosin from actin, and its hydrolysis re-cocks the head. Neither step uncovers the binding sites.

dx: Ebola virus disease with hemorrhage and shock in a returning health care worker
case: A 34-year-old nurse is brought to the emergency department 9 days after returning from caring for patients during an Ebola outbreak in central Africa. She has had 5 days of fever, muscle pain, vomiting, and watery diarrhea, and today has bleeding gums and oozing from a venipuncture site. Temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 78/44 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 38,000/mm3 (normal 150,000 to 400,000), prothrombin time of 19 seconds (normal 11 to 13.5), fibrinogen of 95 mg/dL (normal 200 to 400), markedly elevated D-dimer, AST of 640 U/L (normal 10 to 40), lactate of 6.1 mmol/L (normal 0.5 to 2.2), and creatinine of 2.9 mg/dL (normal 0.6 to 1.2). RT-PCR confirms Ebola virus disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her bleeding?
options: Vitamin K deficiency from poor intake and diarrhea
Antiplatelet antibodies destroying circulating platelets
Isolated loss of hepatic clotting factor synthesis
Consumption of clotting factors in widespread clotting
approach: Read the labs together: low platelets, prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, and high D-dimer.
That combination means clotting and fibrinolysis are both active, so factors and platelets are being used up.
In viral hemorrhagic fevers, infected macrophages and endothelium release cytokines and tissue factor, driving disseminated intravascular coagulation.
questions.why: Viral hemorrhagic fevers share a mechanism: infected monocytes, macrophages, and endothelial cells release a storm of cytokines, express tissue factor, and lose their barrier function. Tissue factor triggers clotting throughout small vessels, which consumes platelets, fibrinogen, and other factors, and fibrin breakdown raises D-dimer. The patient then bleeds from mucosa and puncture sites while also forming microthrombi. Leaky endothelium adds fluid loss and shock. Ebola and Marburg, the filoviruses, spread through blood and body fluids and kill a large share of those infected.
whyNot: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT but does not lower platelets or fibrinogen or raise D-dimer.
Immune thrombocytopenia lowers platelets alone, with a normal PT and fibrinogen.
Liver injury contributes, but loss of synthesis alone would not raise D-dimer or explain the severe thrombocytopenia.
Correct.

questions.stem: The physician compares her illness with dengue hemorrhagic fever, which can look similar. Which of the following features describes the virus that is causing her illness?
options: Negative-sense RNA, fruit bat reservoir, spread by body fluids
Negative-sense RNA, rodent reservoir, spread by aerosolized excreta
Positive-sense RNA, primate reservoir, spread by Aedes mosquitoes
Positive-sense RNA, fruit bat reservoir, spread by body fluids
approach: Classify Ebola: a filovirus, an enveloped, filamentous, negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus.
Recall its natural reservoir, fruit bats, and its spread between people by blood and body fluids.
Contrast with flaviviruses such as dengue and yellow fever: positive-sense RNA spread by Aedes mosquitoes.
questions.why: Ebola and Marburg viruses are filoviruses, long filamentous enveloped viruses with negative-sense single-stranded RNA. Fruit bats are the likely reservoir, and people are infected by contact with blood or body fluids of infected people or animals, which is why health care workers are at risk. Dengue and yellow fever are flaviviruses with positive-sense RNA genomes, spread by Aedes mosquitoes. Severe dengue often follows a second infection with a different serotype, when non-neutralizing antibodies enhance viral entry into macrophages (antibody-dependent enhancement).
whyNot: Correct.
A rodent reservoir with spread by inhaled excreta describes hantaviruses, which can also cause hemorrhagic fever.
This describes flaviviruses such as dengue and yellow fever, which are spread by Aedes mosquitoes.
The bat reservoir and body fluid spread fit Ebola, but filoviruses have negative-sense, not positive-sense, RNA genomes.

questions.stem: Her urine output falls to 10 mL/h, and urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts. Which of the following best explains this kidney injury?
options: Immune complex deposition in glomerular capillaries
Ischemic necrosis of the renal papillae
Hypoperfusion injury of high-demand tubular cells
Direct viral destruction of the collecting ducts
approach: Muddy brown granular casts are shed tubular epithelial cells, the sign of acute tubular necrosis.
Her hypotension and high lactate show progressive shock with poor tissue perfusion.
The straight proximal tubule and thick ascending limb use the most ATP and get the least oxygen, so they die first.
questions.why: In progressive shock, low perfusion pushes cells into anaerobic metabolism, and lactic acidosis develops. In the kidney, the proximal straight tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb have heavy transport work and lie in a relatively low-oxygen region, so they are injured first. Dead tubular cells slough into the lumen, form granular casts, and obstruct flow, causing acute tubular necrosis. Similar hypoperfusion damages the lungs (ARDS) and clotting system (DIC), giving multiorgan dysfunction.
whyNot: Immune complex glomerulonephritis causes red cell casts and hematuria, not muddy brown casts.
Papillary necrosis is linked to analgesic abuse, diabetes, and sickle cell disease and presents with flank pain and sloughed papillae.
Correct.
The collecting ducts are not the main target, and the casts point to ischemic tubular death in shock.

questions.stem: Activated endothelial cells in her small vessels rapidly release the contents of their storage granules, promoting platelet adhesion and leukocyte rolling. Which of the following pairs is released from these granules?
options: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin
von Willebrand factor and P-selectin
Thromboxane A2 and adenosine diphosphate
Heparan sulfate and thrombomodulin
approach: Endothelial storage granules are Weibel-Palade bodies.
Ask which products are prestored and act at once: the adhesion molecules for platelets and leukocytes.
von Willebrand factor tethers platelets, and P-selectin starts leukocyte rolling.
questions.why: Weibel-Palade bodies are rod-shaped endothelial granules that store von Willebrand factor and P-selectin. Within minutes of activation by thrombin, histamine, or inflammatory signals, they fuse with the cell membrane. von Willebrand factor binds platelet glycoprotein Ib to start adhesion, and P-selectin begins leukocyte rolling. Healthy endothelium is antithrombotic, making nitric oxide and prostacyclin on demand and displaying heparan sulfate and thrombomodulin. Injury tips this balance toward clotting and inflammation.
whyNot: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin are made on demand, not stored, and they relax vessels and inhibit platelets.
Correct.
Thromboxane A2 and ADP come from platelets, not endothelial cells.
Heparan sulfate and thrombomodulin are anticoagulant molecules on the endothelial surface, not granule contents.

dx: Mechanical aortic valve with intravascular hemolysis and prosthetic valve endocarditis
case: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of 3 weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue, and dark urine. Eight months ago, his stenotic bicuspid aortic valve was replaced with a mechanical valve, and he takes warfarin. Temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/54 mm Hg. A diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 9.6 g/dL (normal 13.5 to 17.5), reticulocyte count of 5% (normal 0.5 to 2.5), LDH of 820 U/L (normal 140 to 280), and haptoglobin below 10 mg/dL (normal 30 to 200). A blood smear shows schistocytes. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a vegetation on the sewing ring and a paravalvular leak. Blood cultures grow coagulase-negative gram-positive cocci in clusters. Diagnosis: prosthetic valve endocarditis with intravascular hemolysis.

questions.stem: Red cells are fragmented by the high-velocity jet through the paravalvular leak. Which of the following best explains his low serum haptoglobin?
options: Reduced haptoglobin synthesis by an inflamed liver
Haptoglobin binding free hemoglobin for clearance
Haptoglobin loss in the urine through damaged glomeruli
Haptoglobin breakdown by bacterial proteases in the blood
approach: Schistocytes, high LDH, and dark urine show intravascular hemolysis from the abnormal valve.
Haptoglobin is a plasma protein that captures free hemoglobin released from lysed red cells.
The haptoglobin-hemoglobin complex is cleared quickly by macrophages, so haptoglobin levels fall.
questions.why: Mechanical valves, especially with a paravalvular leak, create high-shear jets that tear red cells and produce schistocytes. Free hemoglobin in plasma binds haptoglobin, and macrophages in the liver and spleen take up the complex through the CD163 receptor, so haptoglobin is used up. Once haptoglobin is saturated, free hemoglobin passes into the urine (dark urine), and chronic loss can cause iron deficiency. Haptoglobin is an acute phase protein, so infection alone would tend to raise it.
whyNot: Haptoglobin is an acute phase reactant, so inflammation increases its synthesis.
Correct.
There is no evidence of nephrotic-range proteinuria, and urinary loss is not the usual reason haptoglobin falls in hemolysis.
Bacterial proteases are not a recognized cause of low haptoglobin.

questions.stem: The organism is identified as Staphylococcus epidermidis. Which of the following properties best explains its ability to infect his prosthetic valve?
options: Dextran that binds fibrin-platelet clots
Coagulase that coats the bacterium in a fibrin layer
Protein A binding the Fc region of IgG
Polysaccharide biofilm on foreign surfaces
approach: Note that the organism is coagulase negative and lives on normal skin.
Its main virulence factor is adherence to plastic and metal surfaces inside a slime layer.
Biofilm protects the bacteria from antibiotics and phagocytes, which is why prosthetic infections are hard to cure.
questions.why: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-negative gram-positive coccus in clusters that is part of normal skin flora. It enters at surgery or through lines, then sticks to prosthetic valves, catheters, and joint implants by forming a polysaccharide biofilm. The biofilm shields bacteria from antibiotics and host defenses, so cure often needs valve replacement. Staphylococcus aureus relies instead on coagulase, protein A, and clumping factor, and viridans streptococci use dextran to stick to damaged native valves.
whyNot: Dextran production lets viridans streptococci bind fibrin-platelet deposits on previously damaged native valves.
Coagulase is the defining enzyme of Staphylococcus aureus, and this organism is coagulase negative.
Protein A is a Staphylococcus aureus factor that blocks opsonization.
Correct.

questions.stem: Five days later, his ECG shows a PR interval that lengthens over several days, followed by complete heart block. Echocardiography shows that the infection has spread into an abscess just below the aortic valve. The abscess most likely damaged conducting tissue in which of the following locations?
options: Membranous septum beneath the aortic valve
Moderator band crossing the right ventricle
Upper end of the crista terminalis near the SVC
Subendocardium of the left ventricular apex
approach: Trace the conduction pathway: SA node, atrial muscle, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers.
The AV node lies in the triangle of Koch, and the bundle of His runs through the central fibrous body into the membranous septum.
The membranous septum sits just under the aortic valve, so an aortic root abscess can destroy the His bundle.
questions.why: The impulse starts in the SA node at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium, crosses the atria to the AV node in the triangle of Koch, and is delayed there so atrial contraction can finish filling the ventricles. It then enters the bundle of His, which penetrates the central fibrous body and runs along the membranous interventricular septum directly beneath the aortic valve. Aortic valve endocarditis that spreads into the root can destroy this bundle and cause new heart block, a sign of perivalvular abscess.
whyNot: Correct.
The moderator band carries the right bundle branch. Damage causes right bundle branch block, not complete block.
The SA node lies at the upper end of the crista terminalis. Damage there causes sinus node dysfunction, not AV block.
Purkinje fibers at the apex are distal and widespread, and a local lesion would not block all conduction.

questions.stem: His anemia by itself favors flow murmurs, even in arteries without narrowing. Which of the following changes produced by his anemia most directly increases the tendency toward turbulent blood flow?
options: Increased blood viscosity
Decreased flow velocity
Decreased blood viscosity
Decreased cardiac output
approach: Turbulence is predicted by the Reynolds number, which rises with density, velocity, and diameter and falls with viscosity.
Anemia lowers viscosity because there are fewer red cells.
Anemia also raises cardiac output and velocity, so both changes push flow toward turbulence and flow murmurs.
questions.why: The Reynolds number equals density times velocity times diameter divided by viscosity. Above a critical value, laminar flow breaks into turbulence, which produces murmurs and bruits. His hemoglobin is low, so blood viscosity is low, and the body compensates for anemia with a higher cardiac output and faster flow. Both raise the Reynolds number, explaining flow murmurs without any valve or arterial narrowing.
whyNot: Higher viscosity, as in polycythemia, lowers the Reynolds number and favors laminar flow.
Slower flow lowers the Reynolds number. Anemia speeds flow.
Correct.
Lower cardiac output slows flow and reduces turbulence. Anemia increases output.

dx: Acute type B aortic dissection after heavy weightlifting and cocaine use
case: A 38-year-old man who is a competitive powerlifter is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after sudden, severe, tearing pain between his shoulder blades that began during a maximal deadlift. He used cocaine 2 hours before training. He has untreated hypertension. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 196/112 mm Hg in the right arm and 190/108 mm Hg in the left arm. Lower extremity pulses are present. A chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. CT angiography shows an intimal flap that begins just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery and extends to the level of the renal arteries. The ascending aorta is normal. Diagnosis: acute Stanford type B aortic dissection.

questions.stem: Given the extent of his dissection, he is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?
options: Cardiac tamponade from rupture into the pericardium
Acute aortic regurgitation from loss of cusp support
Kidney or bowel ischemia from branch compression
Myocardial infarction from coronary ostial occlusion
approach: Classify the dissection: it spares the ascending aorta, so it is Stanford type B.
Ask which branches arise from the dissected segment: intercostal, celiac, superior mesenteric, and renal arteries.
The false lumen can compress or shear off these branches, causing malperfusion of the organs they supply.
questions.why: Stanford type A dissections involve the ascending aorta and threaten the structures near the aortic root, causing tamponade, aortic regurgitation, coronary occlusion, and stroke. Type B dissections begin beyond the left subclavian artery and involve only the descending aorta. Their main dangers are rupture and malperfusion, when the expanding false lumen narrows the visceral, renal, spinal, or limb arteries. Type A usually needs emergency surgery, while uncomplicated type B is often managed by tight control of blood pressure and heart rate.
whyNot: Tamponade follows rupture of a type A dissection into the pericardial sac. His ascending aorta is normal.
Aortic regurgitation occurs when a type A dissection undermines the commissures at the aortic root.
Correct.
Coronary ostial occlusion, usually of the right coronary artery, complicates type A dissections.

topics: Stanford type A versus type B

questions.stem: His pain began during a maximal deadlift, a form of static (isometric) exercise. Which of the following best describes the hemodynamic response to this type of exercise compared with dynamic aerobic exercise?
options: Modest rise in arterial pressure with decreased resistance
Large rise in arterial pressure with increased resistance
Fall in arterial pressure with decreased resistance
Unchanged arterial pressure with increased stroke volume
approach: In static exercise, sustained muscle contraction squeezes the vessels in the working muscle.
Resistance in those beds stays high, and the sympathetic pressor response raises heart rate and pressure.
The result is a sharp rise in blood pressure, a pressure load on the left ventricle and aorta.
questions.why: During dynamic exercise such as running, arterioles in active muscle dilate, total peripheral resistance falls, and the higher cardiac output raises systolic pressure only moderately. This is a volume load on the heart. During heavy static exercise, contracting muscles compress their own vessels, peripheral resistance stays high or rises, and a strong pressor reflex drives arterial pressure up steeply. Such abrupt pressure surges, added to cocaine-induced hypertension, raise the shear stress on the aortic wall and can start a dissection.
whyNot: This describes dynamic aerobic exercise, with muscle vasodilation and a volume load.
Correct.
A fall in pressure is not the response to either type of exercise in a healthy person.
Arterial pressure rises during heavy lifting. It does not stay unchanged.

questions.stem: The strength of his aortic wall depends on covalent cross-links between collagen fibrils and between elastin molecules. Which of the following is required by the enzyme that forms these cross-links?
options: Ascorbic acid
Zinc
Selenium
Copper
approach: Name the enzyme that cross-links collagen and elastin: lysyl oxidase.
Recall its cofactor: copper.
Separate this from the earlier hydroxylation step, which needs vitamin C.
questions.why: Lysyl oxidase is a copper-dependent enzyme that converts lysine and hydroxylysine side chains to reactive aldehydes, which then form covalent cross-links in collagen and elastin outside the cell. Copper deficiency, or Menkes disease (a defect in the ATP7A copper transporter), leaves these fibers weak and can cause arterial tortuosity and aneurysms. Vitamin C is needed earlier, inside the cell, for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases; its lack in scurvy causes fragile vessels and bleeding gums.
whyNot: Ascorbic acid is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, which act before triple helix formation, not for cross-linking.
Zinc is a cofactor for many enzymes, including matrix metalloproteinases, but not lysyl oxidase.
Selenium is needed for glutathione peroxidase, and its deficiency is linked to a cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease), not to weak cross-links.
Correct.

questions.stem: Echocardiography shows left ventricular hypertrophy from his untreated hypertension. On a posteroanterior chest radiograph, which of the following parts of the cardiac silhouette is formed by this chamber?
options: Most of the left heart border and the apex
The anterior surface behind the sternum
Most of the right heart border
The upper left border below the aortic knob
approach: Picture the heart's rotation: the right ventricle faces forward and the left ventricle lies to the left and behind it.
On a frontal film, the right border is the right atrium; the left border from top down is the aortic knob, pulmonary trunk, left auricle, and left ventricle.
The apex, at the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, is part of the left ventricle.
questions.why: The heart sits in the middle mediastinum, rotated so the right ventricle forms most of the anterior surface. On a posteroanterior radiograph, the right border is formed mainly by the right atrium, with the superior vena cava above it. The left border is formed from top to bottom by the aortic knob, pulmonary trunk, left auricle, and then the left ventricle, which makes up most of the border and the apex. Left ventricular enlargement therefore extends the left border and shifts the apex outward and downward.
whyNot: Correct.
The anterior surface is mostly the right ventricle.
The right border is formed by the right atrium.
Just below the aortic knob, the upper left border is formed by the pulmonary trunk.

dx: Angiosarcoma of the arm in chronic lymphedema after mastectomy (Stewart-Treves syndrome)
case: A 70-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 3 months of enlarging purple nodules on her left upper arm. Twelve years ago, she had a left mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection and radiation for breast cancer, and since then she has had firm, chronic swelling of the left arm. She takes amlodipine for hypertension. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg. The left arm is swollen and nonpitting, with several violaceous nodules up to 2 cm across, some of which bleed. Biopsy shows irregular, anastomosing vascular channels lined by atypical, mitotically active endothelial cells that stain for CD31. Diagnosis: angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome).

questions.stem: Angiosarcoma also arises in organs other than the skin, linked to specific exposures. Which of the following exposures is a recognized risk factor for angiosarcoma of the liver?
options: Vinyl chloride
Benzene
Aflatoxin B1
Crocidolite asbestos
approach: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of endothelial cells, and her case shows chronic lymphedema as one cause.
Recall the hepatic angiosarcoma exposures: vinyl chloride, arsenic, and the old contrast agent Thorotrast.
Match the other exposures to the tumors they are known for.
questions.why: Angiosarcoma is a rare, aggressive malignant tumor of endothelial cells. It arises in skin and soft tissue of the elderly, in limbs with chronic lymphedema after mastectomy and node dissection, in irradiated fields, and in the liver after exposure to vinyl chloride (used to make PVC plastic), arsenic, or Thorotrast. It grows and spreads quickly, so survival is poor even with treatment.
whyNot: Correct.
Benzene is linked to acute myeloid leukemia.
Aflatoxin is linked to hepatocellular carcinoma, not hepatic angiosarcoma.
Asbestos is linked to mesothelioma and lung carcinoma.

questions.stem: She also has soft, pitting swelling of both ankles that began after she started amlodipine. Her serum albumin is 4.1 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.0), and her urine shows no protein. Which of the following best explains her ankle edema?
options: Decreased plasma colloid oncotic pressure
Increased capillary permeability
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
Obstruction of lymphatic drainage
approach: Amlodipine dilates precapillary arterioles more than venules.
More arterial pressure reaches the capillaries, so capillary hydrostatic pressure rises and more fluid filters out.
The result is a low-protein transudate that pits, unlike her protein-rich, fibrotic, nonpitting arm lymphedema.
questions.why: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers relax arteriolar smooth muscle but have little effect on veins. With the precapillary arterioles open, capillary hydrostatic pressure rises and filtration exceeds lymphatic return, so a transudate collects in dependent tissues. A transudate is low in protein and pits under pressure. An exudate comes from inflamed, leaky vessels and is rich in protein and cells. Her arm swelling is different again: lymphedema retains protein and becomes firm and nonpitting as fibrosis develops.
whyNot: Low oncotic pressure requires low albumin, but her albumin is normal and there is no proteinuria.
Increased permeability produces a protein-rich exudate from inflammation, which is absent here.
Correct.
Lymphatic obstruction explains her arm, but both ankles are affected and the swelling is soft and pitting.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions causes limb swelling by the same mechanism as her chronic left arm swelling?
options: Nephrotic syndrome
Wuchereria bancrofti infection
Right-sided congestive heart failure
Deep vein thrombosis
approach: Identify her mechanism: removal and irradiation of axillary lymph nodes blocked lymph drainage of the arm.
Look for another disease that physically blocks lymphatic vessels.
Adult filarial worms of Wuchereria bancrofti live in and obstruct lymphatics.
questions.why: Lymphedema results when lymphatic drainage fails, from node dissection, radiation, tumor, or infection. Wuchereria bancrofti, spread by mosquitoes, lodges as adult worms in lymphatic vessels, causing inflammation and obstruction that can progress to massive limb swelling (elephantiasis). In all forms, protein-rich fluid builds up, fibrosis develops, and the swelling turns firm and nonpitting. Injury to the thoracic duct, the largest lymph vessel, causes chylothorax instead.
whyNot: Nephrotic syndrome causes edema by lowering plasma oncotic pressure from albumin loss.
Correct.
Right-sided heart failure raises venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure.
Deep vein thrombosis raises venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure in one limb, not lymphatic obstruction.

questions.stem: Before her surgery, lymphatic capillaries in her arm returned filtered fluid and protein from the interstitium. Which of the following structural features normally lets fluid and protein enter these vessels and keeps them open when the tissue swells?
options: Continuous tight junctions over a thick basement membrane
Fenestrated endothelium with diaphragms over the pores
A smooth muscle layer with paired valves along the vessel
Overlapping endothelial flaps with anchoring filaments
approach: Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended tubes of thin endothelium with little or no basement membrane.
Neighboring endothelial cells overlap loosely and act as one-way flap valves.
Anchoring filaments tie the cells to the surrounding tissue, so swelling pulls the flaps open instead of collapsing the vessel.
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries begin as blind ends in the interstitium. Their endothelial cells overlap at loose junctions that open inward when interstitial pressure rises, letting in fluid, protein, and even cells, then close to keep lymph from leaking back out. Anchoring filaments connect the cells to the surrounding connective tissue, so tissue swelling pulls the vessels open. This system returns about 2 to 3 L of filtered fluid and the escaped protein to the blood each day.
whyNot: Continuous tight junctions over a thick basement membrane would block protein entry and describe blood capillaries in places such as the brain.
Fenestrated endothelium with diaphragms is found in blood capillaries of endocrine glands and the gut, not lymphatic capillaries.
Smooth muscle and valves belong to larger collecting lymphatics, which pump lymph forward, not to the capillaries where lymph enters.
Correct.
